title: 14  Large sample test
text:
14.1 Central Limit Theorem
A sample size of 30 or more (\(n≥30\)) is often used as a rough guide to a large sample, but it is not a universal threshold. The required size depends on the population distribution and the statistic being studied. Statistical methods based on such samples are known as large-sample tests. These methods rely on large-sample theory, which uses the Central Limit Theorem to approximate the sampling distribution of test statistics by the normal distribution, even when the population distribution is unknown.
The Central Limit Theorem states that when the sample size is sufficiently large, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, irrespective of the shape of the population distribution, provided the observations are independent and the population has a finite variance.
Mathematically, if a random sample of size \(n\) is drawn from a population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then as \(n\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\infty\),
\[
\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
\xrightarrow{d}
N(0,1),
\tag{14.1}\]
where:

title: 14  Large sample test
text:
\(\bar{X}\) = sample mean
\(\mu\) = population mean
\(\sigma\) = population standard deviation
\(N(0,1)\) = standard normal distribution
\(\xrightarrow{d}\) denotes convergence in distribution. For now just think as “tends to follow” or “approaches” the standard normal distribution as the sample size increases.

title: 14  Large sample test
text:
14.2 Z test
The \(Z\)-test is a statistical test based on the standard normal distribution. It is used to test hypotheses about population means and proportions when the sample size is sufficiently large and the necessary assumptions are satisfied. The value of the test statistic is compared with the critical value from the standard normal distribution to decide whether the null hypothesis should be rejected or not rejected.
The test statistic \(Z\) is calculated from a large sample using appropriate formulas that we will discuss in the coming sections. Under \(H_0\), \(Z\) has an exact or approximate standard normal distribution, \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), depending on the test and its assumptions. The following large sample tests are covered in this chapter:

Test for a single proportion
Test for the equality of two proportions
Test for a single mean
Test for the equality of two means
Test for the difference of two standard deviations


Before applying a test
First identify the population parameter, the sampling unit and whether the samples are independent or paired. Plants measured within the same plot are not necessarily independent experimental replicates. A large number of measurements cannot correct this dependence. The formulas here assume independent observations; substantial sampling fractions or complex survey designs require the corresponding sampling standard errors.
State the alternative hypothesis and the significance level before examining the result. A one-tailed test is used for a specified direction, not because the observed result happens to be positive or negative. Report the estimated difference as well as the decision. A statistically significant difference need not be large enough to be agriculturally important.


14.2.1 Decision rule for the Z test
Let \(Z\) be the calculated value and \(\alpha\) be the level of significance. We reject the null hypothesis if:

\(|Z| > Z_{\alpha/2}\) ; for a two-tailed test
\(Z > Z_{\alpha}\) ; for a right-tailed test
\(Z < -Z_{\alpha}\) ; for a left-tailed test

The critical values of \(Z\) for specified levels of significance are given in Table 14.1.



Table 14.1: Critical values of the standard normal distribution for a one-tailed test





\(\alpha\) (one tail)
\(Z\) value

2.576






For a two-tailed test, the significance level \(\alpha\) is split equally between the two tails, so the critical value corresponds to the one-tail value at \(\alpha/2\). Table 14.2 gives the critical values directly in terms of the overall two-tailed \(\alpha\).



Table 14.2: Critical values of the standard normal distribution for a two-tailed test





\(\alpha\) (two tail)
\(Z\) value

NoteNote



For a two-tailed test at \(\alpha\) = 0.05, we split the significance level equally between the two tails and use the value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is \(Z_{0.025}\) = 1.960. Similarly, for a two-tailed test at \(\alpha\) = 0.01 we use \(Z_{0.005}\) = 2.576. These are the same critical values shown directly against the overall two-tailed \(\alpha\) in Table 14.2.


The same decision can be made using a p-value. It is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) and the test model, of a result at least as extreme as that observed in the direction or directions specified by \(H_1\). It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. Let \(\Phi(z)\) denote the cumulative probability of the standard normal distribution. The p-value is \(1-\Phi(Z)\) for a right-tailed test, \(\Phi(Z)\) for a left-tailed test, and \(2[1-\Phi(|Z|)]\) for a two-tailed test. Reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is at most \(\alpha\).
For example, \(Z=-2.00\) in a two-tailed test gives a p-value of approximately 0.0455. Thus the null hypothesis is rejected at the 5% level. Failure to reject a null hypothesis does not prove equality; the sample may provide insufficient precision to detect a difference.

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.3 Test for a single population proportion
text:
14.3 Test for a single population proportion
Consider a population with proportion \(P\), where \(P\) is unknown. We take a random sample of size \(n\) from the population and calculate the sample proportion \(p\). We want to test whether the population proportion \(P\) is equal to a specified value \(P_0\), based on the sample proportion \(p\). Note here we always frame null hypothesis on population parameter and test using the sample statistics.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(P\) = \(P_0\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(P\) < \(P_0\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(P\) > \(P_0\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(P\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(P_0\) (two-tailed alternative)
For this test, we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{p - P_0}{\sqrt{P_0 Q_0 / n}} \tag{14.2}\]
where \(Q_0 = 1 - P_0\).
When the null hypothesis is true, this \(Z\) approximately follows a standard normal distribution, provided the observations are independent and the expected counts \(nP_0\) and \(nQ_0\) are sufficiently large. A useful introductory guideline is that both counts should be at least 10. If this condition is not met, an exact binomial test can be used.
The calculated value of \(Z\) is then compared with the critical value of \(Z\) from the table of the standard normal distribution. Apply the appropriate one-tailed or two-tailed rule in Section 14.2.1. If the calculated value is less than the table value, we conclude that we do not have enough evidence in our sample to reject the null hypothesis. See Section 14.2.1.






NoteNote



The standard error in the single-proportion test is computed using the null value \(P_0\), giving \(\sqrt{P_0 Q_0/n}\), because the test statistic is derived under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. Some textbooks use the sample-based standard error \(\sqrt{pq/n}\); for large samples the two give very similar results.



Example 14.1 A sample of 500 apples was taken from a large consignment and 60 were found to be bad. Test whether the proportion of bad apples in the consignment is 0.1 or not, at the 5% level of significance.
Solution
Sample size (\(n\)) = 500
Proportion of bad apples in the sample (\(p\)) = 60/500 = 0.12
We want to test whether the proportion of bad apples in the population is 0.1, so \(P_0\) = 0.1 and \(Q_0\) = 1 - 0.1 = 0.9.
The null hypothesis is:
\(H_0\): \(P\) = 0.1
Since we want to test whether the proportion is 0.1 or not, we use a two-tailed test with the alternative hypothesis:
\(H_1\): \(P\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 0.1
The level of significance is 5%, so \(\alpha\) = 0.05.
Now we calculate \(Z\) using Equation 14.2:
\[Z = \frac{p - P_0}{\sqrt{P_0 Q_0 / n}} = \frac{0.12 - 0.1}{\sqrt{0.1 \times 0.9 / 500}}\]
\[= \frac{0.02}{0.01342} = 1.49\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). The calculated value (1.49) is less than the table value (1.960), so we do not have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that there is insufficient evidence to say the proportion of bad apples differs from 0.1.


Exercise 14.1 A random sample of 500 plants was taken from a large experimental field and 65 plants were found to be affected by yellowing disease. Test whether the proportion of affected plants differs significantly from 0.1. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.4 Test for equality of two proportions
text:
14.4 Test for equality of two proportions
Consider two populations with proportions \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), both unknown. We take random samples of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) from the two populations respectively and calculate the sample proportions \(p_1\) and \(p_2\). We want to test whether the population proportions \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are equal, based on the sample proportions.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(P_1\) = \(P_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(P_1\) < \(P_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(P_1\) > \(P_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(P_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(P_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
For this test, we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{p_1 - p_2}{\sqrt{\widehat{P}\,\widehat{Q}\left( \dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)}} \tag{14.3}\]
where \(\widehat{P} = \dfrac{n_1 p_1 + n_2 p_2}{n_1 + n_2}\) is the pooled proportion and \(\widehat{Q} = 1 - \widehat{P}\).
The samples must be independent. For the normal approximation, check that \(n_1\widehat{P}\), \(n_1\widehat{Q}\), \(n_2\widehat{P}\) and \(n_2\widehat{Q}\) are sufficiently large; a useful introductory guideline is at least 10 each. Pooling is used because \(H_0\) specifies a common population proportion.
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately standard normal when the two samples are independent and the expected success and failure counts in each sample are sufficiently large.
The calculated value of \(Z\) is compared with the critical value of \(Z\) from the standard normal table (see Section 14.2.1). If the statistic falls in the rejection region specified in Section 14.2.1, reject \(H_0\). Otherwise, we conclude that we do not have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

Example 14.2 In order to assess the adoption of a new variety of paddy by farmers, a survey was conducted in a locality. The survey covered 80 farmers with large land holdings and 250 farmers with small land holdings. It was observed that 50 of the large-holding farmers and 78 of the small-holding farmers adopted the new paddy variety. Test whether there is any significant difference in the adoption behaviour of the two groups of farmers. (\(\alpha\) = 0.01)
Solution
Sample size of large-holding farmers (\(n_1\)) = 80
Sample size of small-holding farmers (\(n_2\)) = 250
Proportion of large-holding farmers who adopted the variety (\(p_1\)) = 50/80 = 0.625
Proportion of small-holding farmers who adopted the variety (\(p_2\)) = 78/250 = 0.312
We want to test whether the proportion is significantly different between the two populations, so:
\(H_0\): \(P_1\) = \(P_2\)
\(H_1\): \(P_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(P_2\)
This is a two-tailed test.
Step 1: Calculate the pooled proportion.
\[\widehat{P} = \frac{n_1 p_1 + n_2 p_2}{n_1 + n_2} = \frac{80 \times 0.625 + 250 \times 0.312}{80 + 250} = 0.3879\]
\[\widehat{Q} = 1 - 0.3879 = 0.6121\]
Step 2: The level of significance is 1%, so \(\alpha\) = 0.01.
Step 3: Calculate \(Z\) using Equation 14.3.
\[Z = \frac{p_1 - p_2}{\sqrt{\widehat{P}\,\widehat{Q}\left( \dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)}}\]
\[= \frac{0.625 - 0.312}{\sqrt{0.3879 \times 0.6121 \left( \dfrac{1}{80} + \dfrac{1}{250} \right)}}\]
\[= \frac{0.313}{\sqrt{0.2374 \times 0.0165}} = \frac{0.313}{0.06258} = 5.00\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.005, which is 2.576 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (5.00) is greater than the table value (2.576), we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant difference between the two population proportions.

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.5 Test for a single population mean
text:
14.5 Test for a single population mean
Consider a population with mean \(\mu\), where \(\mu\) is unknown. We take a random sample of size \(n\) from the population and calculate the sample mean \(\overline{x}\). We want to test whether the population mean \(\mu\) is equal to a known constant \(\mu_0\), based on the sample mean.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu\) = \(\mu_0\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) < \(\mu_0\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) > \(\mu_0\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_0\) (two-tailed alternative)
This test has two cases:

Case when the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known
Case when the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown


14.5.1 Standard deviation is known
When \(\sigma\) is known, we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x} - \mu_0}{\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}} \tag{14.4}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately standard normal for a sufficiently large independent random sample. For independent normal observations with known population standard deviation, it is exactly standard normal. The decision rule is given in Section 14.2.1.

Example 14.3 A fertilizer packing unit is set to fill bags with a mean weight of 50 kg. From long experience the population standard deviation of the filling process is known to be 3.2 kg. A random sample of 64 bags was drawn and the mean weight was found to be 49.2 kg. Test whether the packing process is working at the intended mean weight of 50 kg, at the 5% level of significance.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\mu\) = 50
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\mu\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 50 (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n\)) = 64
Sample mean (\(\overline{x}\)) = 49.2
Population standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) = 3.2
Population mean (\(\mu_0\)) = 50
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Since \(\sigma\) is known, we use Equation 14.4:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x} - \mu_0}{\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}} = \frac{49.2 - 50}{\dfrac{3.2}{\sqrt{64}}}\]
\[= \frac{-0.8}{0.4} = -2.0\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare \(|Z|\) with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (2.0) is greater than the table value (1.960), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that the packing process is not working at the intended mean weight of 50 kg.



14.5.2 Standard deviation is unknown
When \(\sigma\) is unknown, it is replaced by its sample estimate \(s\), and we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x} - \mu_0}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}} \tag{14.5}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately standard normal for a sufficiently large independent random sample. For a normal population with unknown standard deviation, the statistic has an exact \(t\) distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. The \(t\)-test can therefore be used even when the sample is large. The decision rule is given in Section 14.2.1.

Example 14.4 A sample of 900 items has a mean of 3.4 cm and a standard deviation of 2.61 cm. Test whether the population mean is 3.25 cm at the 5% significance level.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\mu\) = 3.25
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\mu\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 3.25 (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n\)) = 900
Sample mean (\(\overline{x}\)) = 3.4
Sample standard deviation (\(s\)) = 2.61
Population mean (\(\mu_0\)) = 3.25
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Since \(\sigma\) is unknown, we use \(s\) in place of \(\sigma\), applying Equation 14.5:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x} - \mu_0}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}} = \frac{3.4 - 3.25}{\dfrac{2.61}{\sqrt{900}}}\]
\[= \frac{0.15}{0.087} = 1.724\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (1.724) is less than the table value (1.960), we do not have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that there is insufficient evidence to say the mean differs from 3.25 cm.


Exercise 14.2 From a paddy field a sample of 36 plants was selected at random and the panicle lengths were observed. The mean and standard deviation of these measurements were 18.7 cm and 1.25 cm respectively. Test whether the mean panicle length of paddy is 19 cm. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.6 Test for equality of two means
text:
14.6 Test for equality of two means
Let there be two normally distributed populations with means \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) and standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) respectively. Let samples of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be taken from these populations, with sample means \(\overline{x}_1\) and \(\overline{x}_2\). We want to test whether the two population means are significantly different, based on the sample means.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) < \(\mu_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) > \(\mu_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
There are two cases under this test:

Case when the population standard deviations are equal, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma\)
Case when the population standard deviations are not equal, \(\sigma_1 \neq \sigma_2\)


14.6.1 Standard deviations are equal
When the population standard deviations are equal, we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{\sigma \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}}} \tag{14.6}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is exactly standard normal for independent samples from normal populations with known common standard deviation. Otherwise, the normal approximation requires suitable large samples. The decision rule is the same as above (see Section 14.2.1).






NoteNote



If the common \(\sigma\) is unknown, it is replaced by its pooled estimate \(\sqrt{\dfrac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}\), where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the sample sizes and \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) are the sample standard deviations.



Example 14.5 The means of two large samples of sizes 1000 and 2000 members are 67.5 inches and 68 inches respectively. Can the samples be regarded as drawn from the same population with standard deviation 2.5 inches? (Test at the 5% significance level.)
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n_1\)) = 2000
Sample size (\(n_2\)) = 1000
Sample mean of the first group (\(\overline{x}_1\)) = 68
Sample mean of the second group (\(\overline{x}_2\)) = 67.5
Population standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) = 2.5
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Since the two samples are assumed to come from the same population, the standard deviations are equal. We calculate \(Z\) using Equation 14.6:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{\sigma \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}}}\]
\[= \frac{68 - 67.5}{2.5 \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2000} + \dfrac{1}{1000}}}\]
\[= \frac{0.5}{0.0968} = 5.16\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (5.16) is greater than the table value (1.960), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that the population means differ significantly. This test compares means; it does not test every feature of the two population distributions.



14.6.2 Standard deviations are not equal
When the population standard deviations are not equal, we calculate the test statistic \(Z\) using the following formula:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}} \tag{14.7}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is exactly standard normal for independent samples from normal populations with known standard deviations. Otherwise, the normal approximation requires suitable large samples. The decision rule is the same as above (see Section 14.2.1).
If the population standard deviations are unknown, replace them by \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) for a large-sample approximation. Welch’s \(t\)-test in the next chapter also applies and accounts for the estimation of the standard errors. Both samples must contain enough independent observations; a large combined sample size alone is not sufficient.

Example 14.6 Two paddy varieties were compared for their grain yield. A random sample of 100 plots of variety A gave a mean yield of 52 quintals per hectare with a population standard deviation of 8 quintals per hectare, while a random sample of 100 plots of variety B gave a mean yield of 49 quintals per hectare with a population standard deviation of 6 quintals per hectare. The two population standard deviations are known and unequal. Test whether the two varieties differ significantly in mean yield, at the 5% level of significance.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n_1\)) = 100
Sample size (\(n_2\)) = 100
Sample mean of variety A (\(\overline{x}_1\)) = 52
Sample mean of variety B (\(\overline{x}_2\)) = 49
Population standard deviation of variety A (\(\sigma_1\)) = 8
Population standard deviation of variety B (\(\sigma_2\)) = 6
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Since the two population standard deviations are unequal, we use Equation 14.7:
\[Z = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}}\]
\[= \frac{52 - 49}{\sqrt{\dfrac{8^2}{100} + \dfrac{6^2}{100}}}\]
\[= \frac{3}{\sqrt{0.64 + 0.36}} = \frac{3}{1} = 3.0\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare \(|Z|\) with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (3.0) is greater than the table value (1.960), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that the two paddy varieties differ significantly in mean yield.


Exercise 14.3 Two random samples were drawn from two populations and the following data were obtained. Test whether the population means are equal. \(n_1\) = 400, \(n_2\) = 400, \(\overline{x}_1\) = 250, \(\overline{x}_2\) = 220, \(s_1\) = 40, \(s_2\) = 55. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.7 Test for the difference of standard deviations
text:
14.7 Test for the difference of standard deviations
Let there be two populations with standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\). Let samples of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be drawn from these populations, with sample standard deviations \(s_1\) and \(s_2\). We want to test whether the two population standard deviations differ significantly, based on the sample standard deviations.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\sigma_1\) = \(\sigma_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\sigma_1\) < \(\sigma_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\sigma_1\) > \(\sigma_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\sigma_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\sigma_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
The normal-population assumption is important here because the variability of a sample standard deviation depends on the population distribution. For non-normal data, use a method appropriate to that distribution, such as a suitable robust variance comparison, rather than applying this formula automatically.
For independent large samples from normal populations, each sample standard deviation is approximately normally distributed about its population standard deviation, with the standard error of the difference of two sample standard deviations given by
\[\text{S.E.}(s_1 - s_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{2n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{2n_2}} \tag{14.8}\]
Hence, under the null hypothesis, the test statistic is
\[Z = \frac{s_1 - s_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{2n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{2n_2}}} \sim N(0,1) \tag{14.9}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately standard normal for independent large samples from normal populations. The approximation for standard deviations is not justified by the Central Limit Theorem for means alone. The decision rule is the same as above (see Section 14.2.1).
The population standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are usually unknown, and for large samples they are replaced by the corresponding sample standard deviations. The test statistic then reduces to
\[Z = \frac{s_1 - s_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{2n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{2n_2}}} \sim N(0,1) \tag{14.10}\]

Example 14.7 Two large samples of plant height measurements were taken from two fields. Assume independent random samples from normal populations. The first sample of 1000 plants had a standard deviation of 6.0 cm, and the second sample of 1200 plants had a standard deviation of 5.5 cm. Test whether the two populations have equal standard deviations, at the 5% level of significance.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\sigma_1\) = \(\sigma_2\)
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\sigma_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\sigma_2\) (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n_1\)) = 1000
Sample size (\(n_2\)) = 1200
Sample standard deviation of the first sample (\(s_1\)) = 6.0
Sample standard deviation of the second sample (\(s_2\)) = 5.5
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
Since the population standard deviations are unknown, we use Equation 14.10:
\[Z = \frac{s_1 - s_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{2n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{2n_2}}}\]
\[= \frac{6.0 - 5.5}{\sqrt{\dfrac{(6.0)^2}{2(1000)} + \dfrac{(5.5)^2}{2(1200)}}}\]
\[= \frac{0.5}{\sqrt{0.0180 + 0.0126}} = \frac{0.5}{0.1749} = 2.86\]
Since it is a two-tailed test, we compare \(|Z|\) with the critical value at \(\alpha/2\) = 0.025, which is 1.960 (see Section 14.2.1). Since the calculated value (2.86) is greater than the table value (1.960), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that the two populations differ significantly in their standard deviations.


Exercise 14.4 Two random samples gave the following data. Test whether the population standard deviations are equal. \(n_1\) = 800, \(n_2\) = 900, \(s_1\) = 4.2, \(s_2\) = 3.8. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 14  Large sample test
section: 14.8 Confidence intervals for means and proportions
text:
14.8 Confidence intervals for means and proportions
A confidence interval shows the precision of an estimate as well as its magnitude. For a population mean with known standard deviation, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval is
\[\overline{x}\pm Z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.\]
For two independent means with known standard deviations, the interval is
\[ (\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2)\pm Z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}.\]
For unknown standard deviations, the corresponding \(t\) intervals are discussed in the next chapter. Large-sample normal intervals replace the population standard deviations by their sample estimates.
For a single proportion, the simple large-sample interval is
\[p\pm Z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.\]
For the difference of two independent proportions, the corresponding interval is
\[ (p_1-p_2)\pm Z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.\]
Notice that the standard error for the equality test uses the pooled proportion, whereas this confidence interval uses the two sample proportions separately. These simple proportion intervals require adequate success and failure counts and may perform poorly near 0 or 1; score-based intervals, such as the Wilson interval for one proportion, are preferable in those cases. They should not be used automatically for sparse data.
In Example 14.3, the 95% confidence interval is \(49.2\pm1.960(0.4)\), or approximately \((48.42,49.98)\) kg. The intended mean of 50 kg lies outside this interval, agreeing with the two-sided test. A confidence interval describes uncertainty about a population parameter, not the range containing a specified percentage of individual observations.

Quick revision

Large sample → generally \(n\geq30\).
Large-sample tests are based on the Central Limit Theorem.
Central Limit Theorem → sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) approaches a normal distribution as \(n\) increases.
The observations should be independent.
The population should have finite variance.
Large-sample Z-test → based on \(N(0,1)\).
Tests in this chapter → single proportion, equality of two proportions, single mean, equality of two means, and an approximate comparison of two standard deviations under the stated normal-population assumptions.
Single proportion → compare \(P\) with a specified value \(P_0\).
For a single proportion, \(H_0:P=P_0\).
For a single proportion, the alternative may be \(P<P_0\), \(P>P_0\), or \(P\neq P_0\).
Single-proportion standard error uses \(P_0\) and \(Q_0\) under the null hypothesis.
Two proportions → compare \(P_1\) and \(P_2\).
For two proportions, \(H_0:P_1=P_2\).
The two-proportion test uses the pooled proportion \(\widehat{P}\).
Single mean → compare \(\mu\) with \(\mu_0\).
When \(\sigma\) is known, use \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).
When \(\sigma\) is unknown, use \(s/\sqrt{n}\).
Equality of two means → compare \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\).
Equal population standard deviations → use the common \(\sigma\).
Equal but unknown standard deviations → use the pooled estimate.
Unequal population standard deviations → use separate variance terms.
Two-tailed test → reject if \(|Z|>Z_{\alpha/2}\).
Right-tailed test → reject if \(Z>Z_\alpha\).
Left-tailed test → reject if \(Z<-Z_\alpha\).
At \(\alpha=0.05\), two-tailed critical value → \(1.960\).
At \(\alpha=0.01\), two-tailed critical value → \(2.576\).
At \(\alpha=0.05\), right-tailed critical value → \(1.645\).
At \(\alpha=0.05\), left-tailed critical value → \(-1.645\).
The null hypothesis is always stated in terms of the population parameter.
The test statistic is calculated from sample statistics.
If the calculated statistic falls in the critical region, reject \(H_0\).
Otherwise, do not reject \(H_0\).
For a two-tailed test, \(\alpha\) is divided equally between the two tails.
The sign of \(Z\) is important in one-tailed tests; \(|Z|\) is used for the two-tailed decision.
A large absolute value of \(Z\) indicates greater departure from the null hypothesis.

Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

Given \(n=500\), \(p=\frac{60}{500}=0.12\), \(P_0=0.1\), \(Q_0=0.9\). Using Equation 14.2, \(Z=\frac{0.12-0.10}{\sqrt{0.1(0.9)/500}}=1.49\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|1.49|<1.960\), we do not reject \(H_0\). There is insufficient evidence that the proportion of bad apples differs from 0.1.
Given \(n=500\), \(p=\frac{65}{500}=0.13\), \(P_0=0.1\), \(Q_0=0.9\). Using Equation 14.2, \(Z=\frac{0.13-0.10}{\sqrt{0.1(0.9)/500}}=2.24\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|2.24|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence that the proportion of affected plants differs from 0.1.
Given \(n_1=80\), \(n_2=250\), \(p_1=\frac{50}{80}=0.625\), \(p_2=\frac{78}{250}=0.312\). The pooled proportion is \(\widehat{P}=\frac{80(0.625)+250(0.312)}{330}=0.3879\) and \(\widehat{Q}=0.6121\). Using Equation 14.3, \(Z=\frac{0.625-0.312}{\sqrt{0.3879(0.6121)\left(\frac{1}{80}+\frac{1}{250}\right)}}=5.00\). At \(\alpha=0.01\), \(Z_{0.005}=2.576\); since \(|5.00|>2.576\), we reject \(H_0\). There is a significant difference between the adoption proportions of the two groups.
Under \(H_0:P_1=P_2\), the two samples are assumed to come from populations having the same proportion. The pooled proportion \(\widehat{P}=\frac{n_1p_1+n_2p_2}{n_1+n_2}\) provides a common estimate of this population proportion under \(H_0\).
The hypothesized population proportion is 0.20, so \(H_0:P=0.20\). Since the question asks whether the proportion differs from 0.20, \(H_1:P\neq0.20\). This is a two-tailed test.
Given \(\bar{x}=49.2\), \(\mu_0=50\), \(\sigma=3.2\), \(n=64\). Using Equation 14.4, \(Z=\frac{49.2-50}{3.2/\sqrt{64}}=\frac{-0.8}{0.4}=-2.00\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|-2.00|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). The packing process is not working at the intended mean weight of 50 kg.
Given \(n=900\), \(\bar{x}=3.4\), \(s=2.61\), \(\mu_0=3.25\). Since \(\sigma\) is unknown, using Equation 14.5, \(Z=\frac{3.4-3.25}{2.61/\sqrt{900}}=1.724\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|1.724|<1.960\), we do not reject \(H_0\). There is insufficient evidence that the population mean differs from 3.25 cm.
Given \(n=36\), \(\bar{x}=18.7\), \(s=1.25\), \(\mu_0=19\). Using Equation 14.5, \(Z=\frac{18.7-19}{1.25/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-0.3}{0.2083}=-1.44\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|-1.44|<1.960\), we do not reject \(H_0\). There is insufficient evidence that the mean panicle length differs from 19 cm.
Given \(\mu_0=50\), \(\sigma=5\), \(n=100\), \(\bar{x}=48\). Using Equation 14.4, \(Z=\frac{48-50}{5/\sqrt{100}}=\frac{-2}{0.5}=-4\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|-4|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence that the population mean differs from 50.
Given \(\bar{x}=102\), \(\mu_0=100\), \(\sigma=10\), \(n=400\). Using Equation 14.4, \(Z=\frac{102-100}{10/\sqrt{400}}=\frac{2}{0.5}=4\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|4|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence that the population mean differs from 100.
Given \(n_1=2000\), \(n_2=1000\), \(\bar{x}_1=68\), \(\bar{x}_2=67.5\), \(\sigma=2.5\). Using Equation 14.6, \(Z=\frac{68-67.5}{2.5\sqrt{\frac{1}{2000}+\frac{1}{1000}}}=5.16\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|5.16|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). The two samples cannot be regarded as drawn from populations having the same mean.
Given \(n_1=n_2=100\), \(\bar{x}_1=52\), \(\bar{x}_2=49\), \(\sigma_1=8\), \(\sigma_2=6\). Since the population standard deviations are unequal, using Equation 14.7, \(Z=\frac{52-49}{\sqrt{\frac{8^2}{100}+\frac{6^2}{100}}}=\frac{3}{1}=3.00\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|3.00|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). The two paddy varieties differ significantly in mean yield.
The samples are independent and equal variances are not given. Use the large-sample standard error \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}=\sqrt{40^2/400+55^2/400}=3.4004\). Thus \(Z=(250-220)/3.4004=8.82\), which exceeds 1.960. Reject equality of the population means at the two-sided 5% level. Welch’s t-test is also appropriate and gives the same conclusion.
For a two-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.05\), \(\frac{\alpha}{2}=0.025\), so \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\). The critical values are \(-1.960\) and \(1.960\).
For a right-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.01\), \(Z_{0.01}=2.326\); reject \(H_0\) if \(Z>2.326\).
For a left-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.05}=1.645\), so the critical value is \(-1.645\); reject \(H_0\) if \(Z<-1.645\).
For a two-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\). Given \(Z=2.30\), since \(|2.30|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\).
Given \(Z=1.50\). Since \(|1.50|<1.960\), we do not reject \(H_0\).
For a right-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.05}=1.645\). Given \(Z=2.00\), since \(2.00>1.645\), we reject \(H_0\).
For a left-tailed test at \(\alpha=0.05\), \(-Z_{0.05}=-1.645\). Given \(Z=-2.00\), since \(-2.00<-1.645\), we reject \(H_0\).
Given \(n_1=1000\), \(n_2=1200\), \(s_1=6.0\), \(s_2=5.5\). Since the population standard deviations are unknown, using Equation 14.10, \(Z=\frac{6.0-5.5}{\sqrt{\frac{6.0^2}{2(1000)}+\frac{5.5^2}{2(1200)}}}=\frac{0.5}{0.1749}=2.86\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\); since \(|2.86|>1.960\), we reject \(H_0\). The two populations differ significantly in their standard deviations.







CautionHistorical Insights



Why 30? The bell curve, the astronomer, and the birth of large-sample theory
The reason many large-sample tests work traces back to the Central Limit Theorem. For independent, identically distributed observations with finite positive variance, the distribution of the standardised sample mean approaches the standard normal distribution as the sample size grows. The approximation can be slow for strongly skewed or heavy-tailed populations, and dependence requires additional conditions.
The normal curve itself was first derived by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 as an approximation to the binomial distribution, while he was studying games of chance. It was later rediscovered by Carl Friedrich Gauss around 1809, who used it to model the errors astronomers made when measuring the positions of stars and planets. Because the same bell-shaped curve kept appearing whenever many small independent errors were added together, it came to be called the normal distribution, and for a long time the Gaussian distribution. (Gauss 1809)
But where does the familiar cut-off of “\(n\geq30\)” fit? It is a rough teaching convention, not a universal mathematical boundary. For a normal population with unknown standard deviation, the usual mean statistic has an exact t distribution for every sample size greater than one. Its convergence to the normal distribution does not establish that every non-normal sample mean is adequately approximated at 30 observations. (Student 1908)
So the next time you check whether your sample size crosses 30, remember that you are standing on the shoulders of a gambler, an astronomer, and a brewer.








TipQuotes to Inspire



“It is a capital mistake to theorize before one has data.”
- Sir Arthur Conan Doyle







Gauss, Carl Friedrich. 1809. Theoria Motus Corporum Coelestium in Sectionibus Conicis Solem Ambientium. Friedrich Perthes; I. H. Besser.


Student. 1908. “The Probable Error of a Mean.” Biometrika 6 (1): 1–25. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/6.1.1.

title: 15  Small sample tests
text:
15.1 Tests based on Student’s t distribution (t-tests)
The previous chapter introduced large-sample normal approximations. A sample size below 30 is often called small, but 30 is not a universal boundary. The \(t\), \(F\) and \(\chi^2\) distributions used here are also applicable to larger samples when their model assumptions hold. For small samples, those assumptions are especially important.
The \(t\)-distribution is a probability distribution used mainly for statistical inference when the sample size is small and the population standard deviation is unknown. It is similar to the normal distribution but has heavier tails. The distribution with different degrees of freedom is shown in Figure 15.1. As the degrees of freedom increase, the \(t\) distribution converges to the standard normal distribution. \(t\)-statistic can be calculated from the sample using formulas for different situations discussed below.
Figure 15.1: t distribution curves for varying degrees of freedom, compared with the standard normal
Assumptions of the t-test
For independent two-sample tests, observations must be independent both within and between the groups. For the paired test, the pairs must be independent and the normality assumption applies to the within-pair differences. Inspect the observations for strong skewness and unusual values, especially in small samples. If the assumptions are doubtful, a suitable transformation, a randomization test justified by the design, or an appropriate nonparametric method may be needed. Rank tests do not automatically test the same hypothesis about means.

title: 15  Small sample tests
text:
The parent population from which the sample is drawn is normal.
The sample is a random sample, and the observations used as independent units are independent.
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown.



15.1.1 Test for a single population mean
Consider a population with mean \(\mu\), where \(\mu\) is unknown. We take a random sample of size \(n\) from the population and calculate the sample mean \(\overline{x}\). We want to test whether the population mean \(\mu\) is equal to a known constant \(\mu_0\), based on the sample mean.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu\) = \(\mu_0\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) < \(\mu_0\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) > \(\mu_0\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_0\) (two-tailed alternative)
The test statistic is:
\[t = \frac{\overline{x} - \mu_0}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}} \tag{15.1}\]
where \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2}{n - 1}\).
Under the null hypothesis, \(t\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom.


15.1.2 Decision rule for the t test
Let \(t\) be the calculated value, degrees of freedom = \(n - 1\), and \(\alpha\) be the level of significance. We reject the null hypothesis if:

\(|t| > t_{\alpha/2}\) ; for a two-tailed test
\(t > t_{\alpha}\) ; for a right-tailed test
\(t < -t_{\alpha}\) ; for a left-tailed test

Here \(t_{\alpha}\) or \(t_{\alpha/2}\) is obtained from the table of Student’s \(t\) distribution for the given degrees of freedom \(n - 1\) and level of significance \(\alpha\). Use the signed statistic for a one-tailed test and its absolute value for a two-tailed test, as specified above. Otherwise, we do not have enough evidence to reject it. You can see the t-table in Table D.1 of Appendix D

Example 15.1 Based on field experiments, a new variety of green gram is expected to give a yield of 12 quintals per hectare. The variety was tested on 10 randomly selected farmers’ fields. The yields (quintals per hectare) were recorded as 14.3, 12.6, 13.7, 10.9, 13.7, 12, 11.4, 12, 12.6, and 13.1. Do the results confirm the expectation?
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\mu\) = 12
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\mu\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 12 (two-tailed test)
Sample size (\(n\)) = 10
Sample mean, \(\overline{x}\) = \(\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n} = \dfrac{14.3 + 12.6 + \ldots + 13.1}{10} = \dfrac{126.3}{10} = 12.63\)
Sample standard deviation (\(s\)) = 1.0853
\(\mu_0\) = 12
Level of significance, \(\alpha\) = 0.05
The calculation of the sample mean and sample standard deviation is shown in Table 15.1.

\[s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2}{n-1} = \frac{10.601}{9} = 1.1779\]

Exercise 15.1 The mean weekly sales of soap bars in departmental stores were 146.3 bars per store. After an advertising campaign, the mean weekly sales in 22 stores for a typical week was 153.7, with a standard deviation of 17.2. Was the advertising campaign successful? (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 15  Small sample tests
section: 15.2 Test for equality of two means
text:
15.2 Test for equality of two means
Let there be two normally distributed populations with means \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\). Let the population standard deviations be unknown. Let samples of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be taken from these populations, with sample means \(\overline{x}_1\) and \(\overline{x}_2\) respectively. We want to test whether the two population means are significantly different, based on the sample means.
There are two cases under this situation:

Population variances are equal. (Homogeneous variances)
Population variances are unequal. (Heterogeneous variances)

The pooled t-test assumes equal population variances. When this assumption is not justified, Welch’s t-test can be used without a preliminary F-test. Choosing a t-test solely from a preliminary variance test can distort its error rate; the choice should also reflect the study design and the plausibility of the assumptions.

When the population variances are equal (homogeneous)
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) < \(\mu_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) > \(\mu_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
We calculate the test statistic \(t\) using the following formula:
\[t = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{s \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}}} \tag{15.2}\]
where \(s^2 = \dfrac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\) is the pooled variance, and \(\overline{x}_1\) and \(\overline{x}_2\) are the sample means from populations 1 and 2 respectively.
Under the null hypothesis, \(t\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom. The decision rule is the same as for the previous t-test (see Section 15.1.2).


When the population variances are unequal
The Welch t-test is an adaptation of Student’s t-test. It is used to compare the means of two groups when the variances are different.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) < \(\mu_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) > \(\mu_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
We calculate the test statistic \(t\) using the following formula:
\[t = \frac{\overline{x}_1 - \overline{x}_2}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \tag{15.3}\]
where \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) are the sample standard deviations from the two populations respectively.
The degrees of freedom of the Welch t-test are calculated as follows:
\[\text{df} = \frac{\left( \dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2} \right)^2}{\dfrac{s_1^4}{n_1^2 (n_1 - 1)} + \dfrac{s_2^4}{n_2^2 (n_2 - 1)}} \tag{15.4}\]
Once the \(t\) value is determined, read the critical value of Student’s \(t\) distribution from the table corresponding to the significance level. The decision rule is the same as for the previous t-test (see Section 15.1.2).

Example 15.2 Two independent random samples of yields from normal populations have \(n_1=8\), \(\overline{x}_1=24\), \(s_1^2=9\), and \(n_2=10\), \(\overline{x}_2=20\), \(s_2^2=16\). Yield is measured in quintals per hectare. Assuming equal population variances, test whether the population means differ at the 5% level.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2\).
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1:\mu_1\neq\mu_2\) (two-tailed test).
The pooled variance is
\[s^2=\frac{7(9)+9(16)}{8+10-2}=12.9375.\]
Using Equation 15.2,
\[t=\frac{24-20}{\sqrt{12.9375}\sqrt{1/8+1/10}}=2.344.\]
The degrees of freedom are \(8+10-2=16\). The two-tailed 5% critical value is 2.120. Since \(2.344>2.120\), we reject \(H_0\). The population means differ significantly under the stated common-variance model. Equal population variances do not require the two sample variances to be numerically equal.


Example 15.3 Two independent random samples of plots gave the following results: \(n_1=10\), \(\overline{x}_1=25\), \(s_1=4\); \(n_2=12\), \(\overline{x}_2=21\), \(s_2=2\). Yield is measured in quintals per hectare. Assuming normal populations, test whether the population means differ at the 5% level without assuming equal variances.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2\).
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1:\mu_1\neq\mu_2\) (two-tailed test).
Using Equation 15.3,
\[t=\frac{25-21}{\sqrt{16/10+4/12}}=2.877.\]
Using Equation 15.4,
\[\text{df}=\frac{(16/10+4/12)^2}{(16/10)^2/9+(4/12)^2/11}
\approx12.69.\]
The two-tailed 5% critical value is approximately 2.166 and the p-value is approximately 0.0132. Since \(2.877>2.166\), we reject \(H_0\). The estimated difference is 4 quintals per hectare, with a higher mean in the first population. Software can use the fractional degrees of freedom directly. If only a printed table is available, using the next lower available degrees of freedom gives a conservative critical value.


Exercise 15.2 In order to compare the effectiveness of two sources of nitrogen, namely ammonium chloride and urea, on the grain yield of paddy, an experiment was conducted. Assume the treatments were allocated to independent groups of plots. The results on the grain yield of paddy (kg/plot) under the two treatments are given below. Test whether the two sources differ in effectiveness. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)
Ammonium chloride: 13.4, 10.9, 11.2, 11.8, 14, 15.3, 14.2, 12.6, 17, 16.2, 16.5, 15.7
Urea: 12, 11.7, 10.7, 11.2, 14.8, 14.4, 13.9, 13.7, 16.9, 16, 15.6, 16

title: 15  Small sample tests
text:
15.3 Paired t-test
The paired t-test is used to compare the means of two related samples, that is, when we have two values (a pair of values) for the same experimental unit. For example, suppose 20 cows receive a treatment for 3 months and the question is whether the treatment has an impact on milk yield. The milk yield of the 20 cows is measured before and after the treatment. This gives 20 values before treatment and 20 values after treatment. To test whether there is any significant difference between before and after, the paired t-test can be used, because the two sets of values being compared are related. We have a pair of values for each cow, one before and one after treatment.
The number \(n\) in this test is the number of pairs, not the total number of measurements. The differences should be independent between pairs and approximately normal for the exact small-sample test. Two samples of the same size are not paired unless there is a meaningful matching of their observations. In a before-and-after study without a suitable control, a significant change alone does not establish that the treatment caused it.
Suppose we have two correlated random samples \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and \(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n\). We want to test whether the two population means are significantly different.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\mu_1\) = \(\mu_2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be either:
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) < \(\mu_2\) (left-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) > \(\mu_2\) (right-tailed alternative)
\(H_1\): \(\mu_1\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) \(\mu_2\) (two-tailed alternative)
We calculate the test statistic \(t\) using the following formula:
\[t = \frac{\overline{d}}{\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}} \tag{15.5}\]
where \(\overline{d} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i}{n}\), \(d_i = x_i - y_i\), and \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left( d_i - \overline{d} \right)^2}{n - 1}\).
Under the null hypothesis, \(t\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom. For a two-tailed test, we compare \(|t|\) with the critical value. The decision rule is the same as for the previous t-test (see Section 15.1.2).

title: 15  Small sample tests
section: 15.4 Testing the significance of a correlation coefficient
text:
15.4 Testing the significance of a correlation coefficient
Let paired observations follow a bivariate normal population with correlation coefficient \(\rho\). We want to test the null hypothesis that the population correlation coefficient is zero (\(\rho = 0\)). A t-test can be used for this purpose. If we reject the null hypothesis, we conclude that there is a significant correlation in the population (\(\rho \neq 0\)). If we do not have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis, we conclude that there is no significant correlation.
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): \(\rho\) = 0
The alternative hypothesis is:
\(H_1\): \(\rho\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 0 (two-tailed alternative)
The test statistic is:
\[t = \frac{r \sqrt{n - 2}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}} \tag{15.6}\]
Under the null hypothesis, \(t\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom. For the two-tailed alternative, we reject the null hypothesis if \(|t|\) is greater than the table value corresponding to \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom and the level of significance \(\alpha\). In our case \(\alpha\) = 0.05. Under the stated bivariate normal model, this t-test for zero correlation is exact for any sample size \(n>2\).
Fisher’s Z-transformation provides a large-sample approximation useful for confidence intervals and tests involving correlation, including nonzero hypothesised correlations. It does not replace the exact zero-correlation t-test merely because \(n\geq30\). The sample correlation coefficient \(r\) is transformed as:
\[Z = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left( \frac{1 + r}{1 - r} \right) \tag{15.7}\]
Under the null hypothesis \(H_0: \rho = 0\), the statistic \(Z\sqrt{n - 3}\) follows approximately a standard normal distribution. The test statistic is therefore:
\[Z_{\text{cal}} = Z \sqrt{n - 3} \tag{15.8}\]
We reject the null hypothesis if \(|Z_{\text{cal}}|\) exceeds the table value of the standard normal distribution at the chosen level of significance (1.96 at the 5% level, two-tailed).
To test \(H_0:\rho=\rho_0\), where \(-1<\rho_0<1\), use
\[Z_{\text{cal}}=\left[Z-\frac12\ln\left(\frac{1+\rho_0}{1-\rho_0}\right)\right]\sqrt{n-3}.\]
An approximate \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval on the transformed scale is \(Z\pm Z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{n-3}\). Convert each endpoint \(u\) back to the correlation scale using \((e^{2u}-1)/(e^{2u}+1)\). These approximations require independent pairs, a suitable bivariate normal model, \(n>3\) and enough observations for the approximation to be adequate. They are undefined at \(r=1\) or \(r=-1\). A significant Pearson correlation indicates a linear association; it does not establish causation, and a nonsignificant result does not rule out a nonlinear relationship.

Example 15.5 A plant breeder studied the relationship between plant height and grain yield in a sample of 18 rice genotypes and obtained a correlation coefficient of 0.6. Test whether the population correlation coefficient is significant.
Solution
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\rho\) = 0 (population correlation coefficient is zero)
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\rho\) \(\mathbf{\neq}\) 0 (population correlation coefficient is not zero)
Sample correlation coefficient (\(r\)) = 0.6
Number of pairs (\(n\)) = 18
Under the bivariate normal model, the following \(t\) statistic is used to test zero correlation:
\[t = \frac{r \sqrt{n - 2}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}} = \frac{0.6 \sqrt{18 - 2}}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}} = \frac{0.6 \times 4}{\sqrt{0.64}} = \frac{2.4}{0.8} = 3.00\]
\(t_{\text{cal}}\) = 3.00. The table value of \(t\) for \(n - 2 = 16\) degrees of freedom at the 5% level of significance (two-tailed) is 2.120. Since the calculated value is greater than the table value, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant correlation between plant height and grain yield.

title: 15  Small sample tests
text:
15.5 Chi-square test (\(\chi^2\))
If \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots,Z_\nu\) are independent standard normal variables, then \(\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}Z_i^2\) has a chi-square distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom. It takes only nonnegative values, has mean \(\nu\) and variance \(2\nu\), and is positively skewed. The skewness decreases as the degrees of freedom increase.
Chi-square tests are based on the sampling distribution called the chi-square distribution (\(\chi^2\) distribution). The goodness-of-fit and independence tests for categorical counts are based on the following conditions:

The sample observations are independent.
The expected frequencies must be sufficiently large for the chi-square approximation; a total sample size greater than 50 is not a universal requirement.
A common introductory guideline is to have expected frequencies of at least 5. In a goodness-of-fit test, substantively appropriate adjacent categories may be combined, with degrees of freedom adjusted. In contingency tables, categories should not be combined merely to obtain significance; an exact or simulation-based test may be preferable for sparse data.
The constraints on the cell frequencies should be linear, for example \(\sum O_i = \sum E_i\), where \(O_i\) and \(E_i\) represent the observed and expected frequencies.







NoteNote



Chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence tests analyse categorical counts without assuming normally distributed measurements. They still require a specified probability model and suitable expected frequencies. In contrast, the chi-square test for a population variance is a parametric test requiring a normal population.


Degrees of freedom in \(\chi^2\) tests: Degrees of freedom refers to the number of independent variates that make up the statistic. In general, it is the total number of observations less the number of independent constraints imposed on the observations. For example, if \(k\) is the number of independent constraints in a set of data on \(n\) observations, then degrees of freedom = \(n - k\).
Three important chi-square tests are:

Chi-square test for goodness of fit.
Chi-square test for independence of attributes.
Chi-square test for a variance.


15.5.1 Chi-square test for goodness of fit
A very powerful test for the significance of the discrepancy between theory and experiment was given by Prof. Karl Pearson in 1900 and is known as the “\(\chi^2\) test for goodness of fit”. (Pearson 1900)
We want to test the null hypothesis:
\(H_0\): The population category probabilities follow the specified theoretical distribution.
against the alternative hypothesis:
\(H_1\): The population category probabilities do not follow the specified theoretical distribution.
If \(O_i\) (\(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\)) is a set of observed frequencies and \(E_i\) (\(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\)) is the corresponding set of expected (theoretical) frequencies, then Karl Pearson’s chi-square test statistic is:
\[\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\left( O_i - E_i \right)^2}{E_i} \tag{15.9}\]
Here \(O_i\) represents the \(i^{\text{th}}\) observed frequency and \(E_i\) the corresponding expected frequency according to the theory behind the data. Under the null hypothesis, the statistic approximately follows a chi-square distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom when there are \(n\) categories and no parameters are estimated from the data. When \(m\) parameters are estimated by an appropriate fitting method, the usual degrees of freedom are \(n-1-m\).

Decision rule for the goodness-of-fit test
Let \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}}\) be the calculated value and \(\alpha\) the level of significance. Use \(n-1\) degrees of freedom when all category probabilities are specified, or \(n-1-m\) when \(m\) parameters are estimated as described above. We reject the null hypothesis if \(\chi^2_{\text{cal}} > \chi^2_{\text{tab}}\), where \(\chi^2_{\text{tab}}\) is the table value of \(\chi^2\) at the appropriate degrees of freedom. For this goodness-of-fit test, the rejection region is in the right tail. The chi-square test for a population variance can instead be one-sided or two-sided, depending on its alternative.

15.5.2 Chi-square test for independence of attributes
The chi-square test of independence checks whether two attributes are likely to be related. For example, chemical treatment and germination can be two attributes. If we want to know whether chemical treatment has any influence on germination, we can use the chi-square test. For this purpose, the data are arranged in the form of a contingency table.

Expected frequencies
The expected frequency corresponding to each observed frequency \((A_i B_j)\) is calculated from the formula:
\[E_{ij} = \frac{(A_i)(B_j)}{N} \tag{15.10}\]
where \((A_i)\) is the total for class \(A_i\) and \((B_j)\) is the total for class \(B_j\) of the contingency table, and \(N\) is the grand total of all observations.


Degrees of freedom
Degrees of freedom for an \(r \times s\) contingency table = \((r - 1)(s - 1)\).


Test procedure
The null hypothesis to be tested is:
\(H_0\): The two attributes under consideration are independent.
The alternative hypothesis is:
\(H_1\): The two attributes under consideration are not independent.
The test statistic is:
\[\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sum_{j=1}^{s} \frac{\left( O_{ij} - E_{ij} \right)^2}{E_{ij}} \tag{15.11}\]
where \(O_{ij}\) = observed frequencies, \(E_{ij}\) = expected frequencies, \(r\) = number of rows, and \(s\) = number of columns.
It can be verified that \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} \sum_{j=1}^{s} O_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sum_{j=1}^{s} E_{ij}\).
Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic approximately follows a chi-square distribution with \((r - 1)(s - 1)\) degrees of freedom. The decision rule is the same as for the goodness-of-fit test.

The null hypothesis is \(H_0\): the two attributes are independent. The alternative hypothesis is \(H_1\): the two attributes are not independent.
For a 2×2 contingency table, \(\chi^2\) can be found directly using the shortcut formula:
\[\chi^2 = \frac{n\left( ad - bc \right)^2}{C_1 C_2 R_1 R_2} \tag{15.12}\]

Yates’ correction for continuity
Yates’ continuity correction is an optional adjustment to the chi-square approximation for a 2×2 table. Its use is not determined simply by an observed count being less than 5. Adequacy of the approximation depends on expected frequencies; Fisher’s exact test is an alternative for sparse tables. Pooling is generally inappropriate if it removes the scientific comparison of interest. The continuity-corrected statistic, with the correction capped to prevent a negative adjusted discrepancy, is:
\[\chi^2 = \frac{n\left[\max\left(0,\left|ad-bc\right|-\dfrac{n}{2}\right)\right]^2}{C_1 C_2 R_1 R_2} \tag{15.13}\]

15.5.4 Chi-square test for a population variance
Consider a normal population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), where both are unknown. We take a random sample of size \(n\) from the population and want to test whether the population variance \(\sigma^2\) is equal to a known constant \(\sigma_0^2\), based on the sample variance.
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\sigma^2\) = \(\sigma_0^2\)
The alternative hypothesis may be \(H_1:\sigma^2>\sigma_0^2\), \(H_1:\sigma^2<\sigma_0^2\), or \(H_1:\sigma^2\neq\sigma_0^2\).
The test statistic is:
\[\chi^2 = \frac{(n - 1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2} \tag{15.14}\]
where \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left( x_i - \overline{x} \right)^2}{n - 1}\) is the sample variance.
Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic follows a chi-square distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. This exact result requires independent observations from a normal population.
Let \(\chi^2_{\gamma,\nu}\) denote the critical value with probability \(\gamma\) to its right, for \(\nu=n-1\) degrees of freedom. The rejection rules are:

For \(H_1:\sigma^2>\sigma_0^2\), reject if \(\chi^2>\chi^2_{\alpha,\nu}\).
For \(H_1:\sigma^2<\sigma_0^2\), reject if \(\chi^2<\chi^2_{1-\alpha,\nu}\).
For \(H_1:\sigma^2\neq\sigma_0^2\), reject below \(\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\nu}\) or above \(\chi^2_{\alpha/2,\nu}\).

The two-sided critical values are not symmetric because the chi-square distribution is not symmetric. For example, with \(n=15\), \(s^2=12.5\) and \(\sigma_0^2=10\), the statistic is \(14(12.5)/10=17.5\). At the two-sided 5% level, the critical values for 14 degrees of freedom are 5.629 and 26.119. Since 17.5 lies between them, we do not reject \(H_0\).

title: 15  Small sample tests
section: 15.6 F-test for equality of two population variances
text:
15.6 F-test for equality of two population variances
If \(U\) and \(V\) are independent chi-square variables with \(\nu_1\) and \(\nu_2\) degrees of freedom, then \((U/\nu_1)/(V/\nu_2)\) has an \(F\) distribution. The numerator and denominator degrees of freedom must be stated in that order. The distribution takes positive values and is generally positively skewed. Interchanging the variances gives the reciprocal ratio and interchanges the degrees of freedom.
Let there be two normally distributed populations with variances \(\sigma_1^2\) and \(\sigma_2^2\) respectively. Let samples of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be taken from these populations. We want to test whether the two population variances are significantly different, based on the sample variances.
Null hypothesis, \(H_0\): \(\sigma_1^2\) = \(\sigma_2^2\)
Alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\): \(\sigma_1^2\) \(\neq\) \(\sigma_2^2\)
With the population labels fixed in advance, the test statistic is:
\[F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} \tag{15.15}\]
For independent samples from normal populations, this ratio has an \(F\) distribution under \(H_0\), with \(n_1-1\) and \(n_2-1\) degrees of freedom.
The variance-ratio \(F\)-test is sensitive to departures from normality. For non-normal populations, Levene’s test or its median-based form is often more suitable for comparing variances. A large sample alone does not make the exact normal-population \(F\) test valid for arbitrary distributions.

Decision rule for the F-test
For the two-sided alternative, reject \(H_0\) if the ratio is below the lower \(\alpha/2\) critical value or above the upper \(\alpha/2\) critical value. If the larger sample variance is placed in the numerator for convenience, use the upper-tail \(\alpha/2\) critical value with degrees of freedom corresponding to the numerator and denominator samples. A pre-specified one-sided alternative uses the appropriate single tail at level \(\alpha\). The 5% upper-tail F-table is in Appendix E; a two-sided 5% test needs 2.5% upper-tail critical values.

Exercise 15.7 For a random sample from one normal population, \(n_1\) = 11 and \(s_1^2\) = 21.87. For another random sample from a second normal population, \(n_2\) = 8 and \(s_2^2\) = 15.36. Test the equality of variances. (\(\alpha\) = 0.05)

title: 15  Small sample tests
section: 15.7 Confidence interval for a population mean
text:
15.7 Confidence interval for a population mean
A significance test addresses a specified value of a population parameter. A confidence interval also shows the range of parameter values compatible with the data and the assumed model. For independent observations from a normal population with unknown standard deviation, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for the mean is
\[
\bar x\ \pm\ t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n},
\tag{15.16}\]
where \(t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\) is the upper-tail critical value. In Example 15.1, \(\bar x=12.63\), \(s=1.0853\) and \(n=10\). The 95% confidence interval is
\[12.63\pm2.262\frac{1.0853}{\sqrt{10}}
\approx(11.85,\ 13.41)\text{ quintals per hectare}.\]
Because 12 lies within this interval, the corresponding two-sided 5% t-test does not reject \(\mu=12\). A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed population mean in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions; this is not a 95% probability assigned to the fixed mean after the interval has been calculated.
For two independent means, a confidence interval for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) is
\[ (\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2)\pm t_{\alpha/2,\nu}\,\text{S.E.}.\]
For the pooled test, use \(\text{S.E.}=s\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}\) and \(\nu=n_1+n_2-2\). For Welch’s test, use \(\text{S.E.}=\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}\) and the degrees of freedom in Equation 15.4. For paired observations, the interval for the mean difference is \(\overline{d}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}s/\sqrt{n}\), where \(s\) is the standard deviation of the differences. The pooled and paired intervals are exact under their normal models; the Welch interval is approximate.
In Example 15.3, the 95% confidence interval is \(4\pm2.166\sqrt{16/10+4/12}\), or approximately \((0.99,7.01)\) quintals per hectare. It excludes zero, agreeing with the two-sided test.

title: 15  Small sample tests
text:
15.8 Choosing the appropriate test
For one mean with unknown population standard deviation, use the one-sample \(t\)-test. For two independent means, use the pooled test when a common variance is justified, or Welch’s test when it is not. For matched measurements, use the paired test on the differences. Equal sample sizes alone do not determine this choice.
For categorical counts, use goodness of fit to compare one classification with specified probabilities, and a contingency-table test to study association between two classifications. The same contingency-table calculation can compare category proportions across independently sampled groups; this is called a test of homogeneity. Each independent unit must contribute to only one cell. Paired binary observations require a paired method, such as McNemar’s test, rather than the ordinary independence test.
For one normal-population variance, use the chi-square variance test; for the ratio of two independent normal-population variances, use the \(F\)-test. These are different applications from chi-square tests on counts and from the ANOVA \(F\)-test discussed later.
For each test, report the statistic, degrees of freedom where applicable, p-value or critical value, and the conclusion in terms of the population parameter. Also report the estimated effect and a confidence interval where appropriate. Repeated testing of many hypotheses increases the chance of false rejections; a collection of treatment comparisons should be planned and analysed with an appropriate multiple-comparison procedure.
