CautionHistorical Insights



Frank Yates and the art of the missing value
In the field, experiments rarely go exactly to plan. A goat breaks into a plot, a flood washes out a corner, a technician mislabels a sample, and suddenly one of the neatly balanced yields is simply gone. In the early days of agricultural statistics this was a serious problem, because Fisher’s elegant analysis of variance relied on the tidy balance of equal numbers in every treatment and block. A single hole in the data destroyed that balance and, with it, the simple arithmetic of the analysis.
The solution came from Frank Yates, Fisher’s brilliant younger colleague at the Rothamsted Experimental Station. In the early 1930s Yates worked out that a missing observation could be replaced by an estimated value, chosen precisely so as to minimize the error sum of squares, allowing the standard analysis to proceed almost unchanged. His formulae, one for the randomized block design, another for the Latin square, let researchers recover nearly all the information from a damaged experiment with only a small, correctable bias in the treatment sum of squares and the loss of a single degree of freedom. Yates set this out in his 1933 paper on the analysis of replicated experiments with missing values, and the “missing plot technique” quickly became a standard part of every field experimenter’s toolkit. It is a fine example of the statistician’s craft: not discarding hard-won data because of an accident, but finding a principled way to make the most of what remains. (Yates 1933)








TipQuotes to Inspire



“The best time to plan an experiment is after you’ve done it.” - R. A. Fisher







Yates, Frank. 1933. “The Analysis of Replicated Experiments When the Field Results Are Incomplete.” Empire Journal of Experimental Agriculture 1 (2): 129–42.

title: 24  Data transformation
text:
24.1 Logarithmic transformation
Data may require transformation when a suitable model on the original scale does not adequately satisfy the assumptions needed for analysis. A transformation can improve the analysis, but should be chosen from the nature of the response and the model diagnostics.
For the usual exact ANOVA F-tests, the fitted model should have additive effects where assumed, independent errors, constant error variance, and normally distributed errors. Normality concerns errors about the fitted means, rather than the pooled observations from different treatments. Departures differ in their consequences; a transformation cannot repair a lack of independence caused by the design. Residual diagnostics help determine whether a transformation, a different variance model, or another response distribution is appropriate.
A transformation changes the response scale and can change both the scientific quantity being compared and the significance result. Choose it from the response distribution, the scientific question and model diagnostics, rather than to obtain a desired p-value. It does not guarantee that the model assumptions are met.
When analysis uses a transformed response, significance tests and mean comparisons should be performed on that scale. Back-transformed estimates can then be reported in the original units. Examine residual plots for variance patterns, outliers, and departures from normality; a non-significant normality test alone does not establish that all assumptions hold. A back-transformed mean generally differs from the arithmetic mean on the original scale and should be labelled accordingly. For example, back-transforming a mean logarithm gives a geometric mean.
The following are the most commonly used transformations
\((i)\) Logarithmic transformation
\((ii)\) Square root transformation
\((iii)\) Arc sine transformation (Angular transformation)
When the standard deviation is approximately proportional to the positive treatment mean, the coefficient of variation is roughly constant. A logarithmic transformation can improve additivity and variance stability for this multiplicative structure, subject to residual checks.
Logarithms require positive values. For non-negative counts containing zeros, \(\log(Y+1)\) is a common practical choice, but the choice of constant affects the analysis and should be justified. A positive value less than one can be logged directly; its logarithm is negative. Negative observations require a scientifically justified alternative or a shift making every value positive. Common or natural logarithms may be used consistently.

title: 24  Data transformation
text:
24.2 Square root transformation
For Poisson-type counts, the variance is proportional to the mean. A square root transformation can approximately stabilise that variance. For an exact Poisson distribution, variance equals mean; a relationship \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=kE(Y)\) with \(k>1\) describes overdispersion rather than an exact Poisson distribution. Disease counts out of a fixed number of seeds are binomial, not automatically Poisson.
Zero counts can be square-rooted directly. For very small counts, traditional alternatives include \(\sqrt{Y+1}\), \(\sqrt{Y}+\sqrt{Y+1}\), or the Anscombe transformation \(2\sqrt{Y+3/8}\). They are approximations and do not guarantee normally distributed errors. The constant and transformation must be stated and applied consistently.
If \(X=\sqrt{Y+c}\), the inverse is \(Y=X^2-c\). The inverse of a mean on the transformed scale is no greater than the arithmetic mean of the original observations, by concavity of the square root, and the difference need not be small. Adding an appropriate transformed-scale variance is sometimes used as a model-based correction for estimating an original-scale mean. Adding MSE is only an approximation under a specified model; it does not automatically recover the raw mean. Neither square root nor logarithmic data have a universal ranking of how severely they violate ANOVA assumptions.

title: 24  Data transformation
text:
24.3 Angular transformation
This is a traditional transformation for percentage data derived from binomial counts. However, the data like percentage of carbohydrates, percentage of protein, etc need not to be transformed before applying analysis of variance.
If \(a_{ij}\) success out of n trials are obtained in the jth replicate of the ith treatment the sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{ij}=a_{ij}/n\) has variance \(p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})/n\), where \(p_{ij}\) is the underlying success probability. Replacing \(p_{ij}\) by \(\hat{p}_{ij}\) gives an estimate of this variance. Usually these proportions are expressed in percentages. In binomial data variance tends to be small at the two ends of the range of values but larger towards the middle. This tendency also can be used to identify the transformation.
The traditional 30%–70% guideline is only a rough guide for binomial percentages with comparable denominators. It is not a rule that a single percentage outside that range requires transformation. Assess the variance pattern and model residuals. A binomial generalised linear model is another option, especially when denominators differ. If a transformation is used, apply the same transformation to every observation in the analysis.






ImportantNote



The angular transformation is a traditional approximate variance-stabilising transformation for binomial proportions. It does not automatically make the errors normal or the variances equal, particularly with small denominators or proportions near zero or one.


The transformation is obtained by taking the angle whose sine is the square root of the proportion. (percentage / 100) i.e \(arcSin \sqrt p_{ij}\) or \(Sin^{-1} \sqrt p_{ij}\). For \(p_{ij}\) = 0 or 1 (i.e. 0% or 100%) the angular transformation is improved by replacing 0 by 1/4n and 1 by 1-1/4n where, n is the total number of units under observation.

title: 24  Data transformation
text:
24.4 Box-Cox transformation
The logarithmic and square root transformations are related to a wider family of power transformations. For example, a square root uses the power \(1/2\), and a reciprocal uses the power \(-1\). The Box-Cox transformation provides a family indexed by \(\lambda\) for strictly positive responses. The angular transformation is not a member of this family.
The Box-Cox transformation of a variable \(Y\) takes the form
\[
X = \begin{cases} \dfrac{Y^{\lambda}-1}{\lambda}, & \lambda \neq 0 \\ \log Y, & \lambda = 0 \end{cases}
\tag{24.1}\]
where \(Y\) is the untransformed variable, \(X\) is the transformed variable, and \(\lambda\) is the Box-Cox parameter. The value of \(\lambda\) is commonly estimated by maximising the profile likelihood for the fitted model, including the transformation Jacobian. Minimizing unadjusted residual sums of squares across different transformed scales is not a valid selection rule.
Table 24.14 shows how familiar transformations correspond to specific values of \(\lambda\).



Table 24.14: Common values of the Box-Cox parameter \(\lambda\) and their corresponding transformations









\(\lambda\)
Corresponding transformation




1.00
Identity up to a shift: the formula gives \(Y-1\); ANOVA F-tests are unchanged


0.50
Square root transformation


0.33
Cube root transformation


0.25
Fourth root transformation


0.00
Natural logarithmic transformation


-0.50
Reciprocal square root transformation


-1.00
Reciprocal transformation






In practice, fit the model across a suitable range of trial values of \(\lambda\) and compare their profile likelihoods. A nearby simple power may be preferred for interpretation when it is supported by the likelihood. The transformations in Table 24.14 correspond to Box-Cox values up to shifts and nonzero scale factors; at negative powers the formula also reverses the sign relative to a simple reciprocal. These are monotone transformations, so the inverse and interpretation must match the actual formula; at \(\lambda=1\), the formula gives \(Y-1\). Residual diagnostics are still required after choosing the transformation.
The angular examples use degrees. When computing a back-transformation in software whose sine function uses radians, convert \(X\) degrees to \(X\pi/180\) radians before calculating \(100\sin^2(X\pi/180)\).

A treatment has mean 4.2 after the transformation \(X=\sqrt{Y+1}\). Calculate the approximate retransformed value using \(Y=X^2-1\).
A weedicide experiment is conducted in RBD and the weed counts are highly variable. Explain the complete procedure for analysing the experiment after logarithmic transformation.
In a transformed RBD analysis, the treatment effect is significant. Explain how treatment means should be compared.
Explain why the conclusions from transformed data should be interpreted using retransformed means rather than the transformed means alone.
In a percentage mortality experiment, one treatment has 100% mortality in one replication. Explain how this observation should be handled before angular transformation.
A dataset follows the relationship \(\sigma^2=\mu\). Identify the likely distribution and appropriate transformation.
A dataset follows the relationship \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu^2\). Identify the appropriate transformation.
A dataset follows the relationship \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu\). Identify the appropriate transformation.
A dataset follows the relationship \(\sigma^2=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\). Identify the distribution and appropriate transformation.
Explain why applying a transformation to only selected observations is generally inappropriate when the whole dataset requires transformation.
Explain why normality should be checked after transformation before proceeding with ANOVA.
Compare the interpretation of the retransformed means in the three examples given in the chapter.



Important formulae
Logarithmic transformation:
\[
X=\log Y
\]
Logarithmic transformation with a constant:
\[
X=\log(Y+k),\quad k>0
\]
Square root transformation:
\[
X=\sqrt{Y}
\]
Square root transformation when zero values occur:
\[
X=\sqrt{Y+1}
\]
Alternative transformation for very small counts:
\[
X=\sqrt{Y}+\sqrt{Y+1}
\]
Angular transformation:
\[
X=sin^{-1}\sqrt p
\]
where
\[
p=\frac{Y}{100}
\]
Replacement for 0%:
\[
p=\frac{1}{4n}
\]
Replacement for 100%:
\[
p=1-\frac{1}{4n}
\]
Retransformation after logarithmic transformation:
\[
Y=antilogX
\]
Retransformation after \(X=\sqrt{Y+1}\):
\[
Y=X^2-1
\]
Retransformation after angular transformation:
\[
Y=100\times sin^2X
\]
Binomial variance:
\[
\sigma^2=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}
\]
Poisson variance:
\[
\sigma^2=\mu
\]
Empirical variance relationship for square root transformation:
\[
\sigma^2=c^2\mu
\]
Empirical variance relationship for logarithmic transformation:
\[
\sigma^2=c^2\mu^2
\]
Coefficient of variation:
\[
CV=\frac{SD}{Mean}\times100
\]
Critical difference for transformed means in an RBD:
\[
CD=t_{\alpha/2,edf}\sqrt{\frac{2MSE}{r}}
\]


Quick revision

Data transformation → used when the assumptions required for valid statistical analysis are not satisfied.
Main purpose → improve validity, precision, and accuracy of statistical analysis.
Transformation should not be chosen merely to obtain a desired conclusion.
ANOVA and mean separation → performed on the transformed data.
Final means → retransformed to the original scale for interpretation.
Normality → assess model errors using residual diagnostics after transformation.
Transformations covered → logarithmic, square root, angular, and the Box-Cox family.
Logarithmic transformation → suitable when standard deviation is proportional to the mean.
Log transformation → also useful for multiplicative rather than additive effects.
Logarithms require positive inputs; shifts need justification, and an alternative model may be preferable.
Common transformation for zero values → \(\log(Y+1)\).
Positive observations below one can be logged directly; their logarithms are negative.
Square root transformation → appropriate for Poisson-type count data.
Examples → insect counts, number of defectives, and counts of seeds affected by disease.
Poisson distribution → \(\sigma^2=\mu\).
Empirical square root case → \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu\).
Zero counts → \(\sqrt Y\) is defined; the worked example uses \(\sqrt{Y+1}\) consistently.
Retransformation of square root mean → square the value and subtract 1.
Retransformed square root mean → no greater than the original arithmetic mean; the difference may be substantial.
Back-transformed means are not generally arithmetic means; any bias correction must match the fitted model.
Angular transformation → appropriate for percentage data derived from binomial counts.
Binomial variance → \(\sigma^2=p(1-p)/n\).
The 30%–70% guideline is approximate; use the binomial model and residual diagnostics to assess the analysis.
A single proportion outside 30%–70% does not automatically require transformation. If used, apply one transformation consistently.
Angular transformation → \(sin^{-1}\sqrt p\).
For 0% → replace with \(1/(4n)\).
For 100% → replace with \(1-1/(4n)\).
Retransformation of angular mean → \(100\times sin^2X\), using the same angular unit as in the forward transformation.
Percentage of protein, carbohydrate, etc. → need not necessarily be transformed because such percentages are not necessarily binomial proportions.
Distribution and transformation:

Poisson → \(\sqrt{x}\).
Empirical \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu\) → \(\sqrt{x}\).
Binomial → \(sin^{-1}\sqrt p\).
Empirical \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu^2\) → \(\log(x)\).

Logarithmic example → weed counts were transformed using \(X=\log Y\).
Square root example → larval counts containing zero values were transformed using \(X=\sqrt{Y+1}\).
Angular example → insect mortality percentages were transformed using \(X=sin^{-1}\sqrt p\).
In all three examples → ANOVA was performed on transformed values.
Treatment means → compared using the appropriate critical difference after significant treatment F test.
Final interpretation → based on retransformed means expressed in the original units.



Answers to fill in the blanks

1. Transformation 2. Heteroscedasticity 3. Logarithmic 4. Square 5. Arcsine 6. Proportion 7. Transformed 8. Back 9. Squaring 10. Exponentiation 11. Mean 12. Residuals



Solutions to numerical and conceptual questions

Since the standard deviation increases approximately in proportion to the mean, the coefficient of variation is roughly constant across treatments, indicating a multiplicative rather than additive effect. The logarithmic transformation should be used, as it converts multiplicative effects into additive ones and stabilizes the variance in this situation.
If a logarithmic analysis is justified, \(\log(Y+1)\) is one possible choice for nonnegative counts containing zeros, applying it to every observation, including the positive ones, so that all values remain on the same transformed scale.
Using \(X=\sqrt{Y+1}\): for \(Y=0,1,4,9,16\), \(X=1.000,\ 1.414,\ 2.236,\ 3.162,\ 4.123\) respectively.
A square root transformation is a traditional option under the stated Poisson-type model, for which the variance is proportional to the mean, matching the variance-stabilizing property of the square root transformation.
For \(Y=9,16,25,36,49\), \(\sqrt{Y}=3,4,5,6,7\) respectively.
For Poisson-type data the variance is proportional to the mean itself (\(\sigma^2=\mu\)), for which the square root transformation gives approximate variance stability. The logarithmic transformation instead stabilizes variance proportional to the square of the mean (\(\sigma^2=c^2\mu^2\)), which does not match the Poisson case.
For binomial percentages with comparable denominators, the angular transformation is a traditional option. The range 20%–80% alone does not prove it is necessary; examine the variance pattern and residuals, or consider a binomial model.
The percentages satisfy the traditional 30%–70% guideline, so an untransformed analysis may be reasonable with comparable denominators. Residual diagnostics are still needed; the range alone does not establish the assumptions.
One value below 30% does not make transformation compulsory. The appropriate analysis depends on the denominators, mean-variance relationship, and residuals. The angular transformation is a traditional option for binomial proportions; a square root can be useful as an approximation for small proportions near zero.
The 0% observation is replaced by \(\dfrac{1}{4n}\) and the 100% observation is replaced by \(1-\dfrac{1}{4n}\) (expressed as a proportion), where \(n\) is the total number of units on which the percentage was based; the remaining observations (15%, 48%, 76%) are converted directly to proportions and transformed along with the adjusted extreme values, under the angular transformation chosen for this exercise.
\(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{0.25}=\sin^{-1}(0.5)=30^\circ\).
\(\sin^{-1}\sqrt{0.64}=\sin^{-1}(0.8)\approx53.13^\circ\).
\(Y=100\times\sin^2(45^\circ)=100\times0.5=50\%\).
\(X^2-1=4.2^2-1=16.64\).
First take \(X=\log Y\) (or \(\log(Y+1)\) if any weed count is zero) for every observation. Carry out the usual RBD analysis of variance on the transformed values \(X\) to obtain the ANOVA table and test the treatment and block F values. If the treatment effect is significant, calculate the critical difference on the transformed scale and group the transformed treatment means. Finally, retransform the treatment means back to the original scale using \(Y=\text{antilog}\,X\) for interpretation.
The treatment means should first be compared on the transformed scale itself, using the critical difference calculated from the transformed-scale MSE, provided the model diagnostics support the additivity and variance assumptions on that scale; only after this comparison should the means be retransformed to the original scale for reporting.
Back-transformed estimates express the fitted results in the original units and aid interpretation. The transformed scale may itself have a useful scientific meaning, such as log response ratios. A back-transformed mean is generally not the original-scale arithmetic mean, so its interpretation should be stated.
Since 100% mortality occurred in that replication, it should be replaced by \(1-\dfrac{1}{4n}\) (as a proportion) before applying the angular transformation, where \(n\) is the number of insects on which that percentage was based.
The relationship \(\sigma^2=\mu\) is consistent with a Poisson variance function but does not uniquely establish the distribution. For Poisson-type counts, the square root transformation may help stabilize the variance; check the transformed-model residuals.
The relationship \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu^2\) is the empirical case matching the logarithmic transformation.
The relationship \(\sigma^2=c^2\mu\) is the empirical case matching the square root transformation.
This is the variance of a sample proportion from \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials with probability \(p\). The angular transformation gives approximate variance stability for comparable denominators; the variance relationship alone does not uniquely identify a distribution.
ANOVA on transformed data assumes that all the observations have been placed on the same scale; if only some observations are transformed while others are left in the original scale, the resulting values are no longer comparable, and the assumptions of additivity and homogeneity of variance that the transformation was meant to restore would not hold across the whole dataset.
The choice of a transformation (logarithmic, square root, or angular) is based on a general theoretical relationship between the mean and variance for a class of data, but this relationship may not hold exactly for every dataset. Residual diagnostics help assess whether the transformed model is adequate. Neither a transformation nor a non-significant normality test confirms that every ANOVA assumption holds.
The weed example uses logarithms, the larval-count example uses \(\sqrt{Y+1}\), and the mortality example uses angular values in degrees. ANOVA and pairwise comparisons are performed on the transformed scale. Back-transformed estimates aid interpretation but are not generally original-scale arithmetic means. The larval treatments with the largest means, T6 and T5, are not significantly different by the calculated CD; an extreme sample mean need not differ significantly from every other mean.







CautionHistorical Insights



Finding a suitable scale: Box and Cox
In 1964, George E. P. Box and David R. Cox published An Analysis of Transformations. Box was affiliated with the University of Wisconsin, while Cox was at Birkbeck College, University of London. Their paper treated the choice of transformation as part of fitting a statistical model, rather than a rule applied automatically to every dataset. (Box and Cox 1964)
The family indexed by \(\lambda\) connects familiar transformations such as logarithms, square roots and reciprocals. Its value lies in providing a systematic way to examine which scale is supported by the data and model. Choosing a transformation still leaves the researcher responsible for checking the residuals and interpreting the results on the scale actually used.








TipQuotes to Inspire



“It’s easy to lie with statistics. It’s hard to tell the truth without statistics.” – Andrejs Dunkels

Appendix F — Notable personalities in the development of statistics
text:
The science of statistics, as we know it today, is the product of more than three centuries of work by mathematicians, scientists, and thinkers from many countries. What began as political arithmetic, the counting of births, deaths, and trade for the purposes of the state, gradually grew into a rigorous mathematical discipline for reasoning under uncertainty. The following table lists some of the personalities who shaped this journey, from the early students of probability and demography to the founders of modern statistical inference and experimental design. The list is by no means exhaustive; it is meant to give the student a sense of the people and the ideas behind the methods studied in this book.




Table F.1: Some notable personalities in the development of statistics.






Name
Period
Major contribution
Remarks




Pierre de Fermat
1607--1665
With Pascal, developed the early theory of probability through the problem of points (1654).
Co-founder of probability theory


John Graunt
1620--1674
Analysed the London Bills of Mortality and constructed a pioneering life table; pioneer of demography.
One of the founders of political arithmetic


Blaise Pascal
1623--1662
With Fermat, laid the foundations of the mathematical theory of probability.
Co-founder of probability theory


William Petty
1623--1687
Developed political arithmetic, the systematic use of quantitative data for questions of the state.
Co-founder of political arithmetic


Jacob Bernoulli
1655--1705
Proved the Law of Large Numbers in Ars Conjectandi (1713).
Early architect of probability


Thomas Bayes
1701--1761
Formulated Bayes' theorem, the basis of Bayesian inference (published 1763).
Founder of Bayesian statistics


Gottfried Achenwall
1719--1772
Popularised the term Statistik (1749) for the descriptive science of the state.
Associated with the term statistics


Pierre-Simon Laplace
1749--1827
Developed the central limit theorem and Bayesian probability; applied probability to many sciences.
A founder of mathematical probability


Carl Friedrich Gauss
1777--1855
Developed the method of least squares and the normal (Gaussian) distribution of errors.
Normal distribution named after him


Adolphe Quetelet
1796--1874
Applied statistics and the normal curve to social and human data; conceived the average man.
Father of social statistics


Sir Francis Galton
1822--1911
Introduced regression and correlation; pioneered the study of variation and heredity.
Originator of regression and correlation


Francis Ysidro Edgeworth
1845--1926
Advanced statistical theory, correlation and methods of estimation.
Bridged economics and statistics


Karl Pearson
1857--1936
Developed the chi-square test, the correlation coefficient and the method of moments; co-founded Biometrika (1901) and the first university statistics department (1911).
Founder of the biometric school


William Sealy Gosset (Student)
1876--1937
Developed the t-distribution and the t-test for small samples while working at Guinness (1908).
Wrote under the pen name Student


George W. Snedecor
1881--1974
Popularised the analysis of variance and named the F-statistic in Fisher's honour (1934).
Author of Statistical Methods


Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher
1890--1962
Developed analysis of variance (ANOVA), the design of experiments, maximum likelihood and the F-distribution; author of Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925).
Founder of modern statistics


Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis
1893--1972
Introduced the Mahalanobis distance; pioneered large-scale sample surveys; founded the Indian Statistical Institute (1931).
Father of statistics in India


Jerzy Neyman
1894--1981
With E. S. Pearson, developed the theory of hypothesis testing; introduced confidence intervals and the theory of survey sampling.
Co-founder of modern hypothesis testing


Egon Sharpe Pearson
1895--1980
With Neyman, formulated the Neyman--Pearson theory of hypothesis testing.
Co-developer of hypothesis testing


Gertrude Mary Cox
1900--1978
Advanced the design of experiments; co-authored the classic Experimental Designs (1950) with Cochran.
Pioneer of experimental design


Frank Yates
1902--1994
Developed missing-plot techniques, experimental design and the analysis of factorial experiments at Rothamsted.
Pioneer of experimental design


Abraham Wald
1902--1950
Founded statistical decision theory and sequential analysis; applied statistical reasoning to aircraft vulnerability and survivorship bias.
Founder of statistical decision theory


Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao
1920--2023
Gave the Cramer--Rao bound and the Rao--Blackwell theorem; major contributions to estimation theory.
Legend of Indian statistics














NoteNote



The dates given are the years of birth and death. Where a specific discovery is mentioned, the year in parentheses refers to the year of its publication. Many of these workers contributed to several areas of statistics; only their best-known contribution is listed here for brevity.



F.0.1 Agricultural statistics in India
P. V. Sukhatme strengthened the use of random sampling for crop-yield estimation and agricultural surveys. V. G. Panse contributed to agricultural experimentation and training; their jointly authored Statistical Methods for Agricultural Workers helped bring these methods to agricultural researchers.
The ICAR–Indian Agricultural Statistics Research Institute (IASRI) is an institution, rather than an individual personality. Its origins lie in ICAR’s statistical section created in 1930. The section was strengthened with Sukhatme’s appointment in 1940, and the institute received its present name in 1978. Its work links statistical research, teaching, surveys and agricultural applications. (ICAR–Indian Agricultural Statistics Research Institute, n.d.)
The table is selective. Other contributors associated with methods discussed in this book include de Moivre, Poisson, Kolmogorov, Cochran, Spearman, Kendall, Tukey, Duncan and Box.






TipDid you know?



In India, 29 June, the birthday of Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis, is celebrated every year as National Statistics Day in recognition of his contributions to statistics and national planning.
